mainTopic: The end of רבי מאיר's rescue story, the ban on stadiums, theaters and circuses as מושב לצים, and the severity of scoffing
overview: This amud finishes the story of רבי מאיר rescuing the daughter of רבי חנינא בן תרדיון. He proves to the guard that saying 'אלהא דמאיר ענני' brings protection, and later those words save the guard from hanging. The Romans then hunt רבי מאיר. The גמרא gives two versions of how he escaped, and he finally flees to בבל. Next, a ברייתא calls stadiums and besiegers' camps a מושב לצים that leads to ביטול תורה. The גמרא resolves a contradiction with another ברייתא: for the camp it splits the cases, and for stadiums it says the two follow different תנאים, with רבי נתן permitting. A dispute between רבי מאיר and the חכמים about theaters and circuses matters for doing business there. The amud then lists the harsh punishments for scoffing and explains the opening פסוקים of תהלים. A new reading by רבי יונתן begins and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The guard asks how he can be sure the words will save him
steps.stepSummary: The guard doubts that saying 'אלהא דמאיר ענני' will really protect him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And who can say that this is really how it works?
steps.whatsHappening: The guard asks רבי מאיר for proof that the special words will save him. This question sets up the demonstration that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר had promised the guard protection through a short prayer. The guard is risking his life by releasing a prisoner, so he wants evidence before he agrees.

keyTerms.meaning: And who can say? (asking for proof)

phrases.english: And who can say that this is so?
phrases.notes: The guard is speaking. He is asking whether saying 'God of Meir, answer me' will really protect him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי יֵימַר דְּהָכִי אִיכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier part of the story, where רבי מאיר offered the guard money and the protective phrase.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Proof that saying 'אלהא דמאיר ענני' will really save him from danger.

steps.title: רבי מאיר proves it with the man-eating dogs
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר provokes wild dogs, calls out 'אלהא דמאיר ענני', and the dogs leave him alone. The guard then hands over the girl.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You will see right now. There were dogs that used to eat people. He took a clod of earth and threw it at them. They came to eat him, and he said: 'God of Meir, answer me!' They left him alone, and the guard gave her to him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר answers the guard with a live demonstration. He provokes dangerous dogs, says the words, and is saved, so the guard releases the girl.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of arguing, רבי מאיר shows the guard the proof with his own eyes. Once he has seen it work, the guard is convinced and agrees to the deal.

phrases.english: He said to him: Now you will see.

phrases.aramaic: הֲווֹ הָנְהוּ כַּלְבֵי דַּהֲווֹ קָא אָכְלִי אִינָשֵׁי,
phrases.english: There were these dogs that would eat people;
he took a clod of earth and threw it at them.
They were coming to eat him,
he said: "God of Meir, answer me!"
They left him alone, and he gave her to him.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the guard, and 'her' is the daughter of רבי חנינא בן תרדיון, whom רבי מאיר came to rescue.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הַשְׁתָּא חָזֵית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the guard's doubt by showing him the proof directly.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A live demonstration: the dogs leave רבי מאיר alone once he says the words.

steps.title: The guard is saved from hanging by the same words
steps.stepSummary: The government finds out what happened and tries to hang the guard. He says 'אלהא דמאיר ענני' and is saved, and then he tells them the whole story.
steps.simpleTranslation: Eventually the matter was heard in the king's house. They brought the guard and lifted him up to be hanged. He said: 'God of Meir, answer me!' and they took him down. They said to him: What is this? He said to them: This is what happened.
steps.whatsHappening: The promise to the guard comes true when he is about to be executed. Because he explains what happened, the Romans now learn about רבי מאיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words protect the guard just as רבי מאיר promised. His explanation to the Romans is what turns רבי מאיר into a wanted man in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: hanging (being hung up on a pole)

phrases.english: In the end, the matter was heard in the king's house;
they brought him and lifted him up to be hanged.
He said: "God of Meir, answer me!" They brought him down.
They said to him: What is this?
He said to them: This is what happened.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְסוֹף אִשְׁתְּמַע מִילְּתָא בֵּי מַלְכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the promise from step 2 being fulfilled for the guard himself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The guard is miraculously saved from hanging by calling on the God of Meir.

steps.title: The Romans hunt רבי מאיר and he hides in a brothel
steps.stepSummary: The Romans carve רבי מאיר's face at the gate of Rome. When people spot him and chase him, he runs into a brothel.
steps.simpleTranslation: They went and carved רבי מאיר's image at the entrance of Rome, and said: Anyone who sees this face should bring him. One day they saw him and ran after him. He ran away from them and went into a brothel.
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the Romans know who freed the girl, they make a 'wanted' picture of רבי מאיר. He is spotted, chased, and hides in a brothel. This sets up the question of how he escaped.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story turns from the guard back to רבי מאיר, who is now in danger. Hiding in a brothel is the last place anyone would expect to find a great sage. The next two steps give two versions of how he got away.

phrases.english: They went and engraved the image of Rabbi Meir
at the entrance of Rome,

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרִי: כֹּל דְּחָזֵי לְפַרְצוּפָא הָדֵין לַיְיתֵיהּ.
phrases.english: and said: Anyone who sees this face should bring him.
One day they saw him and ran after him;
he ran from before them and entered a brothel.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתוֹ חֲקַקוּ לִדְמוּתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from the guard's story: now the Romans want רבי מאיר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר becomes a wanted man and is forced to hide in a brothel.

steps.title: First version of the escape: pretending to eat gentile food
steps.stepSummary: One opinion says רבי מאיר saw food cooked by gentiles. He dipped one finger in it and licked a different finger, so it looked as if he was eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: He saw food cooked by gentiles. He dipped one finger in it and tasted from another finger.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the first version of how רבי מאיר avoided being recognized. He made it look as if he was eating gentile food, which the Romans knew רבי מאיר would never do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He never actually ate the food. He only faked it by dipping one finger and licking a different one. This tricked the Romans into thinking he could not be רבי מאיר.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי מאיר did not eat בשולי גוים. He dipped one finger and licked a different, clean finger, so he only looked like he was eating.

phrases.english: Some say: He saw food cooked by gentiles,
he dipped with this one and tasted with that one.
phrases.notes: 'This one' and 'that one' are two different fingers. He dipped one in the food and licked the other.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: בִּשּׁוּלֵי גוֹיִם חֲזָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first of two versions of how he escaped from the brothel.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He escaped by pretending to eat gentile food.

steps.title: Second version of the escape: אליהו disguised as a woman
steps.stepSummary: Another opinion says אליהו appeared as a harlot and hugged רבי מאיר. The Romans concluded it could not be רבי מאיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: אליהו came, appeared to them like a harlot, and embraced him. They said: Heaven forbid! If this were רבי מאיר, he would not act this way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the escape. Here אליהו saves him through a disguise, and the Romans decide they have the wrong man.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version רבי מאיר does nothing wrong at all; אליהו only looks like a harlot. The Romans' respect for רבי מאיר's holiness is what convinces them that this man is someone else.

phrases.english: Some say: Elijah came,
appeared to them like a harlot, and embraced him.
They said: Heaven forbid!
phrases.notes: 'They' are the Romans who were chasing him.

phrases.aramaic: אִי רַבִּי מֵאִיר הֲוָה לָא הֲוָה עָבֵיד הָכִי.
phrases.english: If it were Rabbi Meir, he would not act like this.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: אֲתָא אֵלִיָּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A different version of the same escape described in step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He escaped because אליהו disguised himself as a harlot, and the Romans assumed it could not be רבי מאיר.

steps.title: רבי מאיר flees to בבל
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר runs away to בבל. The גמרא gives two opinions about why: because of this story, or because of the story of ברוריא.
steps.simpleTranslation: He got up, fled, and came to בבל. Some say it was because of this incident, and some say it was because of the incident of ברוריא.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with רבי מאיר leaving and going to בבל. The גמרא brings two opinions about what made him leave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One opinion says he fled to escape the Roman danger described here. The other links his leaving to a separate story about his wife ברוריא, which the גמרא only mentions here without telling it.
steps.whatToRemember: The phrase 'אלהא דמאיר ענני' saved both רבי מאיר and the guard. The Romans then hunted רבי מאיר, he escaped (by faking eating gentile food, or through אליהו's disguise), and he finally fled to בבל.

phrases.english: He arose, fled, and came to Babylonia.
Some say: because of this incident,
and some say: because of the incident of Berurya.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָם עֲרַק, אֲתָא לְבָבֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the story by telling us where רבי מאיר ended up.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי מאיר fled to בבל, either because of the Roman danger in this story or because of the ברוריא incident.

steps.title: Stadiums and besiegers' camps are 'the seat of the scornful'
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that going to stadiums or camps of besiegers to watch entertainers is מושב לצים, and it leads to ביטול תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: A person who goes to stadiums or to a besiegers' camp and watches the diviners, spell-casters and all kinds of clowns is sitting in 'the seat of the scornful.' About such people the פסוק says: 'Happy is the man who did not walk... but his delight is in the תורה of ה'.' This teaches that these things lead a person away from learning תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ברייתא: going to these entertainment places counts as מושב לצים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא reads the פסוק in תהלים as a contrast: the man who stays away from the scornful is the one who delights in Torah. So sitting among the scornful takes the place of Torah, and that is ביטול תורה. This ruling is the base text that the next step will challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: Stadiums, where people were killed in fights for entertainment
A camp of soldiers besieging a city
'The seat of the scornful': a place of mockery and empty entertainment

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
One who goes to stadiums or to a camp of besiegers,

phrases.aramaic: וְרָאָה שָׁם אֶת הַנְּחָשִׁים וְאֶת הַחַבָּרִין,
phrases.english: and sees there the diviners and the spell-casters,
bukiyon, mukiyon, muliyon, and luliyon,
phrases.notes: These and the next two words are names for different kinds of clowns and entertainers.

phrases.english: belurin, salgurin —
this is 'the seat of the scornful,'
and about them the verse says:
'Happy is the man who has not walked, etc.'
'but his delight is in the Torah of the Lord.'
So you have learned that these things

phrases.aramaic: מְבִיאִין אֶת הָאָדָם לִידֵי בִּיטּוּל תּוֹרָה.
phrases.english: bring a person to neglect of Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַהוֹלֵךְ לְאִיצְטָדִינִין וּלְכַרְקוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the story of רבי מאיר ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Going to stadiums or besiegers' camps is מושב לצים and leads to ביטול תורה.

steps.title: A second teaching permits going to both places
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא permits stadiums, because one can save a life, and permits besiegers' camps for the town's welfare, as long as he is not counted as one of them. This contradicts the first ברייתא on both points.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they pointed out a contradiction: It is permitted to go to stadiums, because he can shout and save someone. It is permitted to go to a besiegers' camp, because it helps the town, as long as he is not counted as one of them. If he is counted with them, it is forbidden. So the two teachings clash about stadiums, and they clash about the camp!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא that allows what the first one seemed to forbid, and it points out two contradictions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא said both places are מושב לצים. This ברייתא says both are permitted for a good purpose: saving a life at the stadium and helping the town at the camp. So there are two separate contradictions to solve.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And they contradicted it': introduces a source that clashes with the one just quoted
He shouts and saves: he can cry out to spare a condemned person
Be counted as one of them

phrases.english: And they raised a contradiction:
To go to stadiums is permitted,
because he can shout and save someone,
and to go to a camp of besiegers is permitted,
because of the welfare of the town,
as long as he is not counted as one of them,
but if he is counted as one of them, it is forbidden.
There is a contradiction between the two rulings on stadiums,
and a contradiction between the two rulings on the camp!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּרְמִינְהִי: לְאִיצְטָדִינִין מוּתָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 8 with an opposing ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling in step 8 that stadiums and besiegers' camps are forbidden as מושב לצים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A second ברייתא explicitly permits both places, which contradicts the first ברייתא on each point.

steps.title: The camp contradiction is solved, but the stadium one remains
steps.stepSummary: The camp rulings fit together: the first ברייתא means someone counted as one of the besiegers, and the second means someone who is not. The stadium contradiction still stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, the two rulings about the camp do not contradict each other. One is about a person who is counted as one of them, and the other is about a person who is not. But the two rulings about stadiums still contradict each other!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves half the problem and then says the other half is still difficult. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second ברייתא already said that being counted with the besiegers is forbidden, so the first ברייתא can be read as talking about that case. The stadium rulings have no such condition, so they still clash.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Granted': admits one point is fine before pressing on another
'Here... there': splits two sources into two different cases

phrases.english: Granted, camp against camp is not difficult,
here, it is when he is counted as one of them,
there, it is when he is not counted as one of them,
but stadiums against stadiums is still difficult!

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא כַּרְקוֹם אַכַּרְקוֹם לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers part of the challenge in step 9 and then restates the part that remains.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות disagree about the besiegers' camp.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first ברייתא is about one counted with the besiegers. The second is about one who is not.

steps.title: Stadiums: it is a dispute between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The stadium contradiction is a real מחלוקת. The תנא קמא forbids stadiums as מושב לצים, and רבי נתן permits them so a person can save a life or testify that a woman's husband died.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a dispute between תנאים, as it was taught: One may not go to stadiums, because they are 'the seat of the scornful.' רבי נתן permits it for two reasons. First, he can shout and save the person. Second, he can testify for the man's wife so that she is allowed to remarry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the stadium contradiction. The two ברייתות simply follow two different תנאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the גמרא does not reconcile the sources. It admits that they disagree and brings a ברייתא where the dispute appears openly. רבי נתן adds a second reason: even if he cannot save the man, he can be a witness to the death, so the widow is not stuck as an עגונה.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is a dispute between תנאים': the two sources follow different opinions
Testimony about a woman, here that her husband died
To allow her to marry again

steps.whatToRemember: The camp is permitted only if he is not counted as one of the besiegers. Stadiums are a dispute: the תנא קמא forbids them as מושב לצים, and רבי נתן permits them in order to save a life or to testify so a widow can remarry.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי נתן's second reason does not mean he can always save the man. It covers the case where the man is killed anyway: his testimony then frees the wife to remarry.

phrases.english: It is a dispute between Tanna'im,
as it was taught in a baraita:
One may not go to stadiums
because they are 'the seat of the scornful,'

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי נָתָן מַתִּיר מִפְּנֵי שְׁנֵי דְבָרִים:
phrases.english: and Rabbi Natan permits it for two reasons:
one, because he can shout and save someone,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֶחָד, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁמֵּעִיד עֵדוּת אִשָּׁה לְהַשִּׂיאָהּ.
phrases.english: and one, because he can give testimony for a woman to let her remarry.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנָּאֵי הִיא, דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the stadium contradiction left open in step 10.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both ברייתות were assumed to follow one opinion, so they had to agree.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first ברייתא follows the תנא קמא, who forbids stadiums. The second follows רבי נתן, who permits them.

steps.title: Why theaters and circuses are forbidden
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: רבי מאיר forbids theaters and circuses because idol sacrifices are offered there. The חכמים forbid places with sacrifices because of suspected עבודה זרה, and places without sacrifices because they are a מושב לצים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: One may not go to theaters or circuses, because they offer sacrifices there to idols. This is the view of רבי מאיר. The חכמים say: where they offer sacrifices, it is forbidden because people may suspect you of idol worship. Where they do not offer sacrifices, it is still forbidden because it is a 'seat of scorners.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about theaters and circuses. Everyone agrees they are forbidden, but רבי מאיר and the חכמים give different reasons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר gives one reason: idol sacrifices are offered there. The חכמים split it into two cases. Where sacrifices are offered, the problem is חשד עבודה זרה. Where none are offered, the place is still a מושב לצים, the same idea as the stadium ברייתא earlier.

keyTerms.meaning: Suspicion that one is taking part in idol worship
A 'seat of scorners,' a gathering for mockery and empty entertainment

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
One may not go to theaters or circuses,

phrases.aramaic: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁמְּזַבְּלִין שָׁם זִיבּוּל לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה,
phrases.english: because they offer sacrifices there to idols,
phrases.notes: Here מזבלין means offering sacrifices. It is not about fertilizer.

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
And the Rabbis say: a place where they offer sacrifices —
is forbidden because of suspicion of idol worship,
and a place where they do not offer sacrifices —
is forbidden because of "the seat of scorners."

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵין הוֹלְכִין לְטֵרַטְיָאוֹת וּלְקִרְקְסִיאוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the מושב לצים theme from the stadium ברייתות and brings a new ברייתא about theaters and circuses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Theaters and circuses are forbidden. רבי מאיר's reason is idol sacrifices. The חכמים's reason is suspicion of עבודה זרה where sacrifices are offered, and מושב לצים where they are not.

steps.title: What is the practical difference between them?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between רבי מאיר and the חכמים, since both forbid going.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question that sets up the next step. If both sides forbid going, what is left to argue about?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In practice, both opinions end in the same rule: do not go. So the גמרא looks for a case where their different reasons would lead to different results.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the practical difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the ברייתא just quoted in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where the views of רבי מאיר and the חכמים lead to different results.

steps.title: The difference is doing business there
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא מסורא answers that the difference shows up when someone did business at such a place.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא of Sura said: The difference between them is when someone did business there.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא מסורא answers the question. The two views split when a person bought or sold at the theater or circus.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר assumes idol sacrifices definitely happen at these places, so business done there is tied to עבודה זרה. The חכמים connect the place to idol worship only where sacrifices are actually offered. So the status of the business depends on which view you follow.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'carried and gave,' meaning did business
There is a difference between them

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina of Sura said:
The difference between them is one who did business there.

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides forbid going to theaters and circuses. Their argument matters for business done there.
steps.triggerLanguage: נָשָׂא וְנָתַן אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The case of someone who did business at a theater or circus.

steps.title: A puzzle in the פסוק 'אשרי האיש'
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן פזי quotes the opening פסוק of תהלים and points out that its order seems strange. If the man never walked with the wicked, how could he stand or sit with them?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן פזי taught: What does the פסוק mean, 'Happy is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of scorners'? If he never walked with them, how could he stand there? If he never stood, how could he sit? And if he never sat, how could he scorn?
steps.whatsHappening: Since we were just talking about מושב לצים, the גמרא brings a teaching about the פסוק that uses those words. רבי שמעון בן פזי first raises a difficulty with how the פסוק is worded.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק lists three separate things the righteous man avoids: walking, standing and sitting. Each seems to come after the one before it. If he already avoided the first step, praising him for avoiding the later steps seems unnecessary. This question sets up his explanation in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: He expounded (taught a lesson from a פסוק)
What is the meaning of what is written?

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi expounded:
What is the meaning of what is written:

phrases.aramaic: ״אַשְׁרֵי הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר לֹא הָלַךְ בַּעֲצַת רְשָׁעִים
phrases.english: "Happy is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked,
nor stood in the way of sinners,
nor sat in the seat of scorners"?

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי מֵאַחַר שֶׁלֹּא הָלַךְ, הֵיכָן עָמַד?
phrases.english: But since he did not walk, where would he have stood?
And since he did not stand, where would he have sat?
And since he did not sit, where would he have scorned?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מֵאַחַר שֶׁלֹּא הָלַךְ, הֵיכָן עָמַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the halacha of theaters and circuses to an אגדה about the פסוק that uses the words מושב לצים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The wording and order of תהלים 1:1.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Each action seems to depend on the one before it. Once the man avoided walking with the wicked, listing standing, sitting and scorning seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Each small step leads to the next
steps.stepSummary: The answer: the פסוק teaches a slippery slope. Walking with the wicked leads to standing, standing leads to sitting, and sitting leads to scorning. About the scorner, a פסוק in משלי says he alone bears the result.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the פסוק is teaching you this. If he walked with them, he will end up standing. If he stood, he will end up sitting. If he sat, he will end up scorning. And if he scorned, the פסוק says about him: 'If you are wise, you are wise for yourself, and if you scorn, you alone will bear it.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון בן פזי answers his own question. The פסוק is not listing three separate sins. It describes how one small step pulls a person into the next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The order in the פסוק is now the point, not a problem. Walking leads to standing, standing to sitting, and sitting to scorning. The last stage, mockery, brings personal responsibility, as the פסוק in משלי says: the scorner carries the burden alone.

keyTerms.meaning: To tell you (what the פסוק comes to teach)
He will end up, his end is

phrases.english: Rather, it comes to tell you
that if he walked, he will end up standing,
and if he stood, he will end up sitting,
and if he sat, he will end up scorning,
and if he scorned, about him the פסוק says:
"If you are wise, you are wise for yourself,
and if you scorn, you alone will bear it."

steps.whatToRemember: The פסוק 'אשרי האיש' describes a slippery slope. Walking with the wicked leads to standing, then sitting, then scorning. This is why even a small step toward a מושב לצים is dangerous.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why the earlier ברייתות treat simply going to stadiums or theaters so seriously. Being there is the first step toward becoming a scorner.
steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לוֹמַר לָךְ, שֶׁאִם הָלַךְ — סוֹפוֹ לַעֲמוֹד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the difficulty raised in step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the פסוק: the list is a chain of cause and effect, not three separate sins.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק lists three separate sins, so the later ones seem unnecessary once the man avoided the first.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק describes a progression. Each stage leads to the next, and the scorner bears his guilt alone.

steps.title: Scoffing brings suffering
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר teaches that anyone who scoffs will have suffering come upon him, based on a פסוק in ישעיהו.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר said: Anyone who scoffs, suffering comes upon him, as it says: "And now, do not scoff, lest your sufferings grow strong."
steps.whatsHappening: Step 16 ended by saying the scorner bears his own result. Now the גמרא starts a list of statements about what exactly happens to a scoffer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר reads the פסוק as cause and effect: if you scoff, your sufferings get stronger. So suffering is the first punishment named for לצנות.

keyTerms.meaning: Your bonds or disciplines, read here as your sufferings

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer said:
Anyone who scoffs, suffering comes upon him,
as it is said: "And now, do not scoff,"
"lest your sufferings grow strong."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר: כׇּל הַמִּתְלוֹצֵץ יִסּוּרִין בָּאִין עָלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands on the scorner mentioned at the end of step 16 by naming his punishment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A scoffer is punished with suffering.

steps.title: רבא begs his students not to scoff
steps.stepSummary: רבא puts רבי אליעזר's teaching into practice and pleads with the רבנן not to scoff, so that suffering won't come on them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to the Rabbis: Please, I ask of you that you not scoff, so that suffering will not come upon you.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא takes the idea from step 17 and turns it into a personal, heartfelt request to his own students.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds nothing new to the law. It shows how seriously a great teacher took the danger in step 17: he speaks in the language of pleading, not just teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: Please, I beg you (a polite request)

phrases.english: Rava said to the Rabbis:
Please, I ask of you
that you not scoff,
so that suffering will not come upon you.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רָבָא לְרַבָּנַן: בְּמָטוּתָא בָּעֵינָא מִינַּיְיכוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Practical application of רבי אליעזר's teaching in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Avoid scoffing so that suffering does not come.

steps.title: Scoffing shrinks one's livelihood
steps.stepSummary: רב קטינא says a scoffer's food and livelihood get smaller, based on a פסוק in הושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב קטינא said: Anyone who scoffs, his livelihood is lessened, as it says: "He drew back His hand from scorners."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second punishment for scoffing: losing one's livelihood.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב קטינא reads "drawing back the hand" as ה׳ pulling back the hand that feeds a person. The result is that scoffers end up with less sustenance.

phrases.english: Rav Katina said:
Anyone who scoffs, his livelihood is lessened,
as it is said: "He drew back His hand with scorners."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב קַטִּינָא: כָּל הַמִּתְלוֹצֵץ מְזוֹנוֹתָיו מִתְמַעֲטִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second punishment for scoffing alongside the suffering in step 17.

steps.title: A scoffer falls into גיהנם
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן לקיש says a scoffer falls into גיהנם. He learns this from a פסוק in משלי, explained through a word link to a פסוק in צפניה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן לקיש said: Anyone who scoffs falls into גיהנם, as it says: "A proud, haughty man, scorner is his name; he acts in arrogant wrath." And "wrath" means nothing other than גיהנם, as it says: "That day is a day of wrath."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third and harsher punishment for scoffing: falling into גיהנם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in משלי calls the person a scorner (לץ) and says he acts with עברה, wrath. A second פסוק uses עברה for the day of judgment, so עברה is taken to mean גיהנם. Together they show that the scorner ends up in גיהנם.

keyTerms.meaning: Gehinnom, the place of punishment after death
This word means nothing other than... (a defining formula)

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said:
Anyone who scoffs falls into Gehinnom,
as it is said: "A proud, haughty man, scorner is his name,"
"he acts in arrogant wrath,"
and "wrath" means nothing other than Gehinnom,
as it is said: "That day is a day of wrath."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ: כׇּל הַמִּתְלוֹצֵץ נוֹפֵל בְּגֵיהִנָּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third, harsher punishment for scoffing.

steps.title: A haughty person falls into גיהנם
steps.stepSummary: רבי אושעיא uses the exact same פסוקים, but says they are about the haughty person, not only the scoffer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אושעיא said: Anyone who is haughty falls into גיהנם, as it says: "A proud, haughty man, scorner is his name; he acts in arrogant wrath." And "wrath" means nothing other than גיהנם, as it says: "That day is a day of wrath."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אושעיא repeats the same proof as step 20 but applies it to a different person: someone who acts arrogantly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק mentions both יהיר (haughty) and לץ (scorner). ריש לקיש focused on the word לץ, and רבי אושעיא focuses on the word יהיר. Same verse, different key word.

keyTerms.meaning: One who acts haughty or arrogant

steps.confusionAlert: This step looks like a copy of step 20, but one word is different: מתייהר (haughty) instead of מתלוצץ (scoffer). That one word is the whole point.

phrases.english: Rabbi Oshaya said:
Anyone who is haughty falls into Gehinnom,
as it is said: "A proud, haughty man, scorner is his name,"
"he acts in arrogant wrath,"
and "wrath" means nothing other than Gehinnom,
as it is said: "That day is a day of wrath."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא: כׇּל הַמִּתְיַיהֵר נוֹפֵל בְּגֵיהִנָּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same proof as step 20 but applies it to haughtiness instead of scoffing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A haughty person falls into גיהנם.

steps.title: Scoffing brings destruction on the world
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנילאי בר חנילאי says scoffing causes destruction for the whole world. He reads the rest of the same פסוק in ישעיהו from step 17.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנילאי בר חנילאי said: Anyone who scoffs causes destruction to the world, as it says: "And now, do not scoff, lest your sufferings grow strong, for I have heard of destruction, firmly decreed."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the most extreme effect of scoffing: it doesn't just hurt the scoffer, it brings destruction on the world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר in step 17 used only the first half of the פסוק (sufferings). רבי חנילאי continues to the second half, which speaks of a decreed destruction. So the damage of scoffing reaches beyond the person himself.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanilai bar Chanilai said:
Anyone who scoffs causes destruction to the world,
as it is said: "And now, do not scoff,"
"lest your sufferings grow strong,"
"for I have heard of destruction, firmly decreed."
phrases.notes: Same ישעיהו 28:22 as step 17. This time he reads on to the end of the פסוק.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִילַאי בַּר חֲנִילַאי: כׇּל הַמִּתְלוֹצֵץ גּוֹרֵם כְּלָיָיה לָעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reads the end of the same פסוק used in step 17 to show an even greater consequence.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Scoffing causes destruction to the world.

steps.title: Scoffing starts with suffering and ends with destruction
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר sums up how severe scoffing is: its beginning is suffering and its end is destruction.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר said: It is severe, for its beginning is suffering and its end is destruction.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר wraps up the list by joining the two halves of the ישעיהו פסוק into one picture.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first half of the פסוק spoke of sufferings (step 17), and the second half spoke of destruction (step 22). רבי אליעזר says these are two stages of one sin. That is what makes scoffing so serious.
steps.whatToRemember: Scoffing (לצנות) is treated as a very serious sin. It brings suffering, loss of livelihood and גיהנם, and in the end it can bring destruction on the world.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer said:
It is severe,
for its beginning is suffering and its end is destruction.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר: קָשָׁה הִיא שֶׁתְּחִילָּתוֹ יִסּוּרִין וְסוֹפוֹ כְּלָיָיה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Combines step 17 (suffering) and step 22 (destruction) into one summary.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Scoffing begins with suffering and ends with destruction.

steps.title: Reading the first פסוק of תהלים as a warning against gentile entertainment
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן פזי explains each part of תהלים 1:1. Not walking means not going to theaters and circuses. Not standing means not standing at animal fights. Not sitting with scorners means not sitting among schemers.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן פזי expounded: "Happy is the man who has not walked" to the theaters and circuses of gentiles. "Nor stood in the way of sinners" is one who did not stand at animal-fight shows. "Nor sat in the seat of scorners" is one who did not sit among schemers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the topic of theaters and circuses from step 12. It uses the same פסוק from תהלים that רבי שמעון בן פזי discussed in step 15.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each verb in the פסוק is matched to a real place. Walking matches theaters and circuses, standing matches the animal-fight arena, and sitting matches a gathering of scoffers. This ties the whole discussion of לצנות back to the ban on going to those places.

keyTerms.meaning: Arena for animal fights or hunting shows

steps.whyThisMatters: It closes the circle. The talk about scoffers grew out of the ban on theaters and circuses, and now the פסוק itself is read as warning against exactly those places.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi expounded:
"Happy is the man who has not walked"
to the theaters and circuses of gentiles;
"nor stood in the way of sinners"
this is one who did not stand at the animal-fight arena;
"nor sat in the seat of scorners"
one who did not sit among schemers.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּרַשׁ רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן פַּזִּי: אַשְׁרֵי הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר לֹא הָלַךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the list of punishments and returns to theaters and circuses, reading תהלים 1:1 as a warning against them.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The three parts of תהלים 1:1 warn against theaters and circuses, animal-fight arenas, and gatherings of schemers.

steps.title: Avoiding bad places is not enough; you must learn Torah
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן פזי finishes his teaching. Someone might think that skipping theaters and animal fights means he can sleep all day. תהלים 1:2 says you must learn תורה day and night.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person might say: "I didn't go to theaters or circuses, and I didn't stand at animal fights, so now I'll just go and enjoy sleeping." That is why the פסוק says: "And in His תורה he meditates day and night."
steps.whatsHappening: The teaching from step 24 continues. It raises a mistake someone could make and uses the next פסוק to correct it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 24 listed only things to avoid. Here the drasha adds a positive duty: the empty time must be filled with תורה. The proof comes from פסוק 2, which follows the 'don't' list of פסוק 1.

keyTerms.meaning: Lest a person say. This sets up a mistaken idea so the פסוק can correct it.
I will indulge myself in sleep

steps.whatToRemember: Running away from bad things is only half the job. The other half is filling your time with תורה.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how the drasha reads the two פסוקים together: פסוק 1 lists what to avoid, and פסוק 2 says what to do instead.

phrases.english: Lest a person say:
Since I did not go to theaters and circuses
and I did not stand at animal fights,
I will go and indulge in sleep,
therefore the פסוק teaches:
"And in His Torah he meditates day and night."

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁמָּא יֹאמַר אָדָם הוֹאִיל וְלֹא הָלַכְתִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רבי שמעון בן פזי's drasha from step 24 by moving from פסוק 1 to פסוק 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Avoiding scoffers' gatherings is not enough. One must actively learn תורה day and night.

steps.title: A new reading of 'Happy is the man' begins
steps.stepSummary: רב שמואל בר נחמני, in the name of רבי יונתן, starts a different explanation of תהלים 1:1. The explanation is cut off at the word 'this' and continues later.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: "Happy is the man who did not walk in the counsel of the wicked". This is...
steps.whatsHappening: A new אמורא begins a second explanation of the same פסוק. This line only sets it up; the actual explanation comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון בן פזי read the פסוק as places to avoid. Now רבי יונתן is about to give a different reading, starting with the words 'this is'. We have to wait for the next part to hear what he says.

keyTerms.meaning: This [refers to]. It introduces an explanation.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן:
phrases.english: Rav Shmuel bar Naḥmani said that Rabbi Yonatan said:
"Happy is the man
who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked"
phrases.notes: תהלים 1:1. This is the same פסוק from step 24, now being read a new way.

phrases.english: this is
phrases.notes: The sentence keeps going on the next part of the daf, where we find out who 'this' is.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, different reading of the same פסוק that רבי שמעון בן פזי explained in step 24.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Opens רבי יונתן's own reading of תהלים 1:1. The content continues in the next part of the daf.
